title: Do Credit Guarantees Create Value?
abstract: This paper studies whether credit guarantees create value, and who receives it. Using 2011–2016 SBA 7(a) loans with secondary-market price data, we measure risk-adjusted profit (RAP) for the SBA and for lenders. Following an exogenous fee-relief policy shift intended to expand credit access, SBA RAP falls by 1.75 cents per guaranteed dollar. While lender RAP on fee-waived loans rises by 1.34 cents per loan dollar, we find no direct evidence of borrower benefits such as reduced interest spreads, larger loan amounts, or higher aggregate lending. We show how lenders realize gains from the fee shift. They exploit the guarantee wedge by shifting contracts toward greater guarantee protection, and our evidence indicates that about 25 percent of the loan-size compression toward the higher guarantee is driven by lenders' own incentives.
